Terephthalate and its |FRAME: CPD-19189 "dimethyl ester"| have very low toxicity, with LD50s on the order of grams/kg |CITS: [Sheehan00]|.

bp:smallMolecule.bp:COMMENT: Ethylene glycol is commonly used as a coolant, as a deicing fluid, and to produce plastics such as polyethylene terephthalate. Eethylene glycol readily partitions into the aqueous phase, resulting in high mobility and rapid dispersion through the biosphere. Although the toxicity is low |CITS: [11302583]|, acute exposure can result in kidney and brain damage and possibly teratogenesis.
bp:smallMolecule.bp:NAME: ethylene glycol

bp:protein.bp:COMMENT:
The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1547922|, isolated from sediment at a |FRAME: CPD-19188| (PET) bottle recycling site, was shown to use PET as its major energy and carbon source |CITS: [26965627]|.
Genome sequencing has identified a gene, |FRAME: G-44601|, that encodes a |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.101|, and enzyme that hydrolyzes PET to produce |FRAME: CPD-19187| (MHET). Expression analysis revealed another gene, |FRAME: G-44602|, with similar expression levels in four different media as the |FRAME: G-44601| gene. The sequence of |FRAME: G-44602| matches |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.20|, which is known to hydrolyze the ester linkage of aromatic compounds such as gallic acid esters.
The gene was synthesized using codon optimization for expression in |FRAME: TAX-562| with an N-terminal His<sub>6</sub> tag, and the recombinant protein was purified and shown to hydrolyze |FRAME: CPD-19187| to |FRAME: TEREPHTHALATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOL| |CITS: [26965627]|.
The crystal structures of active ligand-free enzyme was reported at a resolution of 2.05 Å. The structures of the enzyme bound to a non-hydrolyzable MHET analogs (mono-(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalamide and benzoate) were reported at a resolution of 2.1 and 2.2 Å, respectively.
The enzyme possesses a classic α/β-hydrolase domain and a lid domain conferring substrate specificity, similar to the structures of that of feruloyl esterases. The presence of a structural calcium-binding site was confirmed by X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy. Mutation of the enzyme generated a version that is active with |FRAME: CPD-22500| (BHET) |CITS: [30979881]|.
bp:protein.bp:NAME: mono(ethylene terephthalate) hydrolase

bp:smallMolecule.bp:COMMENT:
Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is the most common thermoplastic polymer resin of the polyester family and is used in fibers for clothing, containers for liquids and foods, thermoforming for manufacturing, and in combination with glass fiber for engineering resins. In the context of textile applications, PET is referred to by its common name, polyester.
PET, which consists of polymerized units of the monomer |FRAME: CPD-19187|, is the fourth-most-produced polymer, surpassed only by polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP) and polyvinyl chloride (PVC).
bp:smallMolecule.bp:NAME: polyethylene terephthalate

bp:protein.bp:COMMENT: The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1547922|, isolated from sediment at a |FRAME: CPD-19188| (PET) bottle recycling site, was shown to use PET as its major energy and carbon source |CITS: [26965627]|. Genome sequencing has identified a gene, |FRAME: G-44601|, that encodes a putative lipase. The gene shares 51% amino acid sequence identity and catalytic residues with a hydrolase from |FRAME: TAX-2021| that exhibits PET-hydrolytic activity |CITS: [Ribitsch12]|. The gene was synthesized using codon optimization for expression in |FRAME: TAX-562| with a C-terminal His6 tag, and the recombinant protein was purified and shown to hydrolyze |FRAME: CPD-19188| in vitro |CITS: [26965627]|. In vivo, the organism, which adheres to PET, secretes the enzyme to afford the degradation of the substrate. The enzyme can bind to PET, even though it lacks any carbohydrate-binding modules |CITS: [26965627]|. The crystal structures of the protein were initially reported at a resolution of 1.58 and 1.5 Å, respectively, revealing two intra-molecular disulfide bridges and a Ser-His-Asp catalytic triad at its active site. The substrate binding site is optimized to accommodate four monohydroxyethyl terephthalate (MHET) moieties of PET |CITS: [29235460][29374183]|. A subsequent study reported the structure at a resolution of 0.92 Å. It was also reported in that study that the enzyme also degrades another semiaromatic polyester, |FRAME: CPD-22498| (PEF) |CITS: [29666242]|. Based on the structural information provided by the crystal structure, several mutants were constructed (S93M, W159F, and N241F ) that can hydrolyze naphthyl esters |CITS: [30502092]|.
bp:protein.bp:NAME: poly(ethylene terephthalate) hydrolase

bp:pathway.bp:COMMENT:
|FRAME: CPD-19188 "Polyethylene terephthalate"| (PET) is the most common thermoplastic polymer resin of the polyester family and is used in fibers for clothing, containers for liquids and foods, thermoforming for manufacturing, and in combination with glass fiber for engineering resins. In the context of textile applications, PET is referred to by its common name, polyester.
PET, which consists of polymerized units of the monomer |FRAME: CPD-19187|, is the fourth-most-produced polymer, surpassed only by polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP) and polyvinyl chloride (PVC). About 56 million tons of PET were produced in 2013 alone. PET is chemically inert, making its accumulation in the environment a global concern.
Degradation of PET is limited to a few fungal and bacterial species. A number of cutinases, lipases, and esterases active on PET have been identified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-169388|, |FRAME: TAX-5541|, |FRAME: TAX-5062|, |FRAME: TAX-300|, and |FRAME: TAX-2021| |CITS: [21076908]|.
The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1547922|, isolated from sediment at a PET bottle recycling site, was shown to use PET as its major energy and carbon source. The key enzymes used by the organism are |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.101|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.102|, which together convert the polymer into |FRAME: TEREPHTHALATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOL| monomers, which are environmentally benign |CITS: [26965627]|.
|FRAME: TAX-1547922| harbors a gene cluster that is highly similar to the two |FRAME: TEREPHTHALATE| degradation gene clusters that have been previously identified in |FRAME: TAX-364029|, suggesting that |FRAME: TEREPHTHALATE| is degraded further as described in |FRAME: PWY-7795| |CITS: [16517628]|.
bp:pathway.bp:NAME: polyethylene terephthalate degradation

bp:protein.bp:NAME: leaf-branch compost cutinase
bp:protein.bp:COMMENT:
In 2012 a gene encoding a cutinase homolog was cloned from a fosmid library prepared from a metagenome DNA isolated from compost of a leaf-branch meterial. The enzyme was named LCC for Leaf-branch Compost Cutinase |CITS: [22194294]|.
The gene was cloned with the pelB leader sequence and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, resulting in excretion of more than 50% of the recombinant enzyme into the extracellular medium, from which it was purified. The enzyme hydrolyzed various fatty acid monoesters with acyl chain lengths of 2 to 18, with a preference for short-chain substrates, at an optimal temperature of 50 °C. In addition, the enzyme degraded poly(ε-caprolactone) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET). Its PET degradation rate of 12 mg/h/mg of enzyme was better than other enzymes known at the time |CITS: [22194294]|.
The crystal structure of the enzyme was reported at 1.5 Å resolution. The authors found that the enzyme is a kinetically robust protein, and that the active site is protected from a heat-induced local conformational change by binding of PET. The thermodynamic and kinetic stability of the enzyme was dependent on a single disulfide bond between Cys275 and Cys292 |CITS: [24593046]|.
A comparison of several PET-hydrolyzing enzymes performed in 2020 found that LCC outperformed all other enzymes tested, reaching an initial depolymerization rate of 93.2 mg TAeq/h/mg of enzyme at 65 °C (where TAeq stands for equivalents of |FRAME: TEREPHTHALATE|). When using bottle-grade PET, the initial depolymerization rate went down to 81.9 mgTAeq/h/mg of enzyme |CITS: [32269349]|.
The researchers used targeted mutagenesis to improve avtivity and temperature resistance. While native LCC is thermally stabilized by the addition of calcium ions, the researchers replaced the metal-binding site with a new disulfide bridge, allowing thermal stabilization without dependence on calcium ions. Combined with additional mutations that were found to improve activity and thermal stability, an improved form of the protein was able to achieve 90% depolymerization over 10 hours, making it superior to other enzymes known at the time, such as the |FRAME: MONOMER-19898| from |FRAME: TAX-1547922| |CITS: [32269349]|.
